title: Cloudy before school
note: Fictional child. Values are illustrative; your pediatric PD pathway and the pediatric nephrologist’s orders come first.
intro: You are on the pediatric PD hotline. At 6:30 a.m., Mrs. Joy Castillo calls. Her son Paolo, 8 years old and 24 kilograms, is on automated PD with a dry day. The first drain of the morning looks cloudy, he says his tummy hurts, and he feels warm. They live 40 minutes from the hospital by tricycle and jeepney, and he has a test at school today.

choices.text: Screen for sepsis now: how he looks and behaves, his temperature, breathing, color, vomiting, drinking and urine.
choices.feedback: Cloudy fluid with pain is possible peritonitis. Before you plan anything else, find out whether he is unstable. An unstable child goes to emergency care now, not to the PD clinic later.

choices.text: Tell her to discard the bag, send him to school, and call if tonight’s drain is cloudy too.
choices.feedback: Discarding the bag loses the first sample, and waiting a day lets peritonitis advance. Peritonitis is the main reason children leave PD.
choices.then: You call back at once, ask her to keep the bag, and start the screen.

choices.text: Ask her to bring him to the clinic when it opens at nine, with the bag.
choices.feedback: Keeping the bag is right, but you have not yet asked whether he is safe to wait. Screen first.
choices.then: You go back and ask the screening questions.

vitals.screen: Alert, drinking, no vomiting, abdomen sore

n2.scene: Paolo is alert and talking. He is drinking water, has not vomited, and passed urine this morning. His temperature is 38.2 °C, and his abdomen hurts when he moves. His hands are warm.

choices.text: Come to the hospital now, by the route your pathway names, bringing the closed cloudy bag upright and his medicine list; call the pediatric nephrologist with SBAR and tell the receiving team he is coming.
choices.feedback: He is stable for now, but peritonitis needs sampling and antibiotics this morning. Bringing the bag closed and upright preserves the sample, and SBAR lets the nephrologist decide where he is seen.

choices.text: He looks well: school first, then the clinic this afternoon.
choices.feedback: A stable child still needs prompt treatment. Antibiotics should start as soon as possible after specimens, and delays are linked with worse outcomes.
choices.then: You change the plan: hospital now, nephrologist informed.

choices.text: Give paracetamol and see whether the fever settles before deciding.
choices.feedback: Paracetamol hides the fever without treating the infection and costs hours. You do not recommend medicines that are not on his plan.
choices.then: You change the plan: hospital now, nephrologist informed.

n3.scene: Paolo arrives at 7:45 a.m. The bag split on the way and is no longer a usable sample. His abdomen has been empty since the morning drain because he has a dry day.
n3.prompt: How should the effluent sample be obtained?

choices.text: Per protocol and the nephrologist’s order, instill a fill and let it dwell at least 2 hours before sampling for cell count, differential, Gram stain and culture.
choices.feedback: The 2024 ISPD pediatric guideline’s rationale asks for at least a 2-hour dwell in a child on APD without a daytime dwell, so that white cells collect and the count is meaningful.

vitals.sample: Fill in 7:55; sample at 9:55 per order

choices.text: Instill a fill, drain it after 10 minutes, and send that.
choices.feedback: A 10-minute dwell is too short for cells to collect. A falsely low count can delay the diagnosis.
choices.then: The nephrologist asks for a fill with a proper dwell; the sample is taken after 2 hours.

vitals.sample: Fill in 8:10; sample at 10:10 per order

choices.text: Skip the effluent sample and ask for antibiotics now.
choices.feedback: Speed matters, but without a valid sample the team cannot confirm the diagnosis or choose the right antibiotic. The nephrologist decides how to balance sampling and timing.
choices.then: The nephrologist orders a fill with a 2-hour dwell, with blood cultures and a plan for the first dose.

vitals.sample: Fill in 7:55; sample at 9:55 per order

n4.scene: The sample is cloudy. A resident asks whether to wait for the cell count before the antibiotics the nephrologist has ordered.
n4.prompt: What do you say, within your role?

choices.text: The specimens are taken, so start the ordered antibiotics now, by the ordered route; I will record the sample time and the first-dose time.
choices.feedback: Antibiotics should start as soon as possible after appropriate specimens. The intraperitoneal route is preferred when the drugs allow; agents and doses are the nephrologist’s.

choices.text: Wait for the culture result tomorrow so we treat the right organism.
choices.feedback: Cultures take a day or more. Empiric therapy starts now and is adjusted when the culture returns.

choices.text: Wait the 30 minutes for the cell count, then start.
choices.feedback: Two of the four criteria (cloudy fluid with pain, and fever) are already present, so the empiric diagnosis stands. The count confirms; it should not hold up the first dose.
choices.then: The first dose goes in after the count returns.

n5.scene: Paolo is comfortable. His mother asks, close to tears, whether this happened because she did something wrong.

choices.text: Reassure her without blame, explain the plan and warning signs, and record that the team will do an apparent cause analysis and a retraining review, which peritonitis triggers.
choices.feedback: Every episode gets an apparent cause analysis, and peritonitis is a retraining trigger. Framing it as a system check keeps the family reporting honestly.

choices.text: Tell her peritonitis usually means the caregiver broke technique.
choices.feedback: Blame makes families hide problems, and the cause is not yet known. It may be the exit site, the bowel or a contamination at any step.
choices.then: You apologize, explain the review, and book retraining as a routine step.

choices.text: Say it was bad luck and nothing needs to change.
choices.feedback: Kind, but it skips the cause analysis and retraining review that help prevent the next episode.
choices.then: You add the review and retraining check to the plan.

end.title: Treated within hours
end.text: Paolo is on treatment by mid-morning, with antifungal prophylaxis as ordered, and goes home with a follow-up visit, warning signs and a retraining review booked. You record the call time, screen, arrival, sample time and dwell, first-dose time and the plan.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Screen before you plan. Stability decides emergency care now or urgent hospital care this morning; neither is “wait and see”.
  • Two of four make the diagnosis. Cloudy fluid with pain and fever already meet the ISPD 2024 pediatric criteria.
  • Dry day, longer dwell. A child on APD without a day dwell needs at least a 2-hour dwell before sampling.
  • Specimens, then antibiotics without delay. The count and culture confirm and guide; they do not hold up the first dose.
  • No blame. Every episode gets an apparent cause analysis and a retraining review.
